newsitem.title: USA: Surprise US March core PPI jump helps unsettle mkt.
newsitem.headline: Surprise US March core PPI jump helps unsettle mkt.

text.p: A surprise jump in the core U.S. inflation rate for March combined with a stronger U.S. first-quarter retail sales picture than economists had envisioned appeared to raise chances for another Federal Reserve interest rate hike in May and helped to send bond prices lower on Friday, economists and market analysts said.

"The Producer Price Index (PPI) was a little bit of a shock because the core (the PPI without its more volatile food and energy components) was up 0.4 percent," said James Glassman, senior economist at Chase Securities Inc.

The government reported two pieces of economic news at the same time on Friday. The Labor Department reported that producer prices slipped 0.1 percent overall, but that the closely watched core PPI jumped 0.4 percent.

Meanwhile, the Commerce Department reported a 0.2 percent rise in retail sales for March, softer than economists had anticipated. But Commerce also revised January and February retail sales figures upward. February sales were revised to a gain of 1.5 percent, almost double the 0.8 percent rise first reported. And January sales were revised up to a 1.7 percent increase, from a 1.5 percent gain originally reported.
"This kind of news takes us closer to a tightening, but it's more the retail sales trends than the PPI trends," said Glassman.
The financial markets have become accustomed to seeing moderate price trends, so the reaction to any sharp price jumps is asymmetric, he said.
"When people see low inflation, they say, 'Oh, more of the same.' But rising inflation news is a problem, because everyone knows that's the risk," Glassman said.

Glassman and other analysts noted that about half of the jump in the core PPI was due to price increases in items like tobacco and aircraft. The price increases on the latter item, at least, would not transfer into the closely watched Consumer Price Index (CPI), they said.
"The core PPI you can explain away -- it was aircraft and tobacco," said Josh Stiles, senior bond strategist at I.D.E.A.
But at least in March, core prices at the intermediate and crude stages of production appeared to be moving away from their long-term flat to negative trends.
At the intermediate stage of production, the core PPI was unchanged. And at the earlier, crude production levels, the core PPI index jumped 0.6 percent.

"These (retail sales and producer price) numbers suggest that the economy does have momentum, that the Fed was right to tighten and ... (suggest) that further interest rate increases are going to be necessary to change the tide for the economy," said Matthew Alexy, chief markets strategist at Credit Suisse First Boston. Alexy said that if the March CPI, due next week, is "like this PPI result, it would be lights out and we would be at 7.25 percent very fast in the long bond (yield)."
